blogPosts.title: How Long Does It Take to Build a Web or Mobile App?
blogPosts.excerpt: Realistic timelines for an MVP, an internal tool and a full platform, what moves them, and how to shorten them without cutting corners.
blogPosts.coverAlt: Abstract illustration of a project timeline
blogPosts.content:
"How long will it take?" is the first question in almost every discovery call, and the honest answer is a range, not a date. This post gives you the ranges we actually quote, what pushes a project to the top or bottom of each range, and what you can do before kick-off to land on the short side.

## The short version

- A focused **MVP or internal tool**, web or mobile, usually takes **4 to 8 weeks** from kick-off to production.
- A **platform** with several apps, roles and third-party integrations usually takes **2 to 4 months**.
- Mobile apps add **store review time** on top: typically a day or two for the App Store, and up to a week for a new Google Play developer account.
- A **rescue or performance project** on an existing codebase is measured in weeks, not months, because the first fixes are usually architectural, not a rewrite.

These are the numbers behind the answers on our [services page](/services). They assume one small team that owns design, web, mobile and backend together. Splitting the work across three vendors adds coordination time that no estimate can hide.

## What actually sets the timeline

Features are only one input. In practice five things decide where a project lands inside a range.

- **How many decisions are already made.** A project with a clear owner, a written list of what is out of scope, and a decision on the first user flow moves twice as fast as one where every screen is a debate. Discovery exists to make those decisions early.
- **Integrations.** Each payment provider, CRM, ERP or partner API adds its own sandbox, its own quirks and its own approval process. Three integrations can cost as much as the rest of the product.
- **Roles and permissions.** An app with one kind of user is simple. An app with customers, operators and admins who each see different things needs a permission model, and that model touches every screen.
- **Design readiness.** If a design system or brand already exists, we build straight into it. If not, the first one or two weeks produce the screens that everything else depends on.
- **Mobile specifics.** Offline mode, background sync, push notifications and store compliance are not add-ons. Each one is a week of work and testing on real devices.

## Typical ranges, by project type

**Marketing site or landing pages: 1 to 3 weeks.** Content and design are the long pole, not code. Passing Core Web Vitals is part of the definition of done, not a later optimisation.

**Internal tool or dashboard: 3 to 6 weeks.** One or two user roles, a database, a handful of screens and an authentication layer. These are the fastest projects to ship and the ones that pay back first.

**MVP of a web or mobile product: 4 to 8 weeks.** A real product, deliberately small: one core flow done well, analytics, crash reporting and a release pipeline from day one. The point is to learn from real users in week eight, not to launch everything in month six.

**Platform or multi-app product: 2 to 4 months.** A web app, a mobile app and the backend they share, with integrations and several user roles. We phase these: a usable first release in the first six to eight weeks, then increments on top.

**Rescue, audit or performance work: 2 to 6 weeks.** A profiling pass, a written list of what is slow or fragile, then fixes in order of impact. A ground-up rewrite is almost never the answer, which is why this is measured in weeks.

## How we estimate

- **Discovery call, 30 to 45 minutes.** What you are building, who uses it, and what it costs the business if it fails.
- **Written scope.** A short document: what we will build, what we will leave out on purpose, the phases, the timeline and the price. Not a 40-page proposal.
- **Phases, not a single deadline.** Each phase ends with working software on a staging link or a test build, so the plan gets corrected every week or two instead of at the end.

## How to shorten the timeline without cutting corners

- Name one decision-maker on your side and keep feedback rounds short.
- Write down what the first release does *not* include. Every item on that list is a week saved.
- Bring the accounts early: app store developer accounts, domain access, payment provider and API keys. Waiting for a login is the most common idle week in any project.
- Prefer boring, proven technology. Exotic choices cost time twice: once to build and again to maintain.
- Launch the smallest version that real users can use, then iterate. Month eighteen matters more than launch day.

## Get a real estimate

Tell us what you are building through the [project form](/start-project) or write to [hello@alaz.pro](mailto:hello@alaz.pro). After a short call you get a written scope with phases, a timeline and a price, usually within a week. Every message is read by an engineer, and we reply within one business day.

blogPosts.title: What Does a Slow Website Actually Cost Your Business?
blogPosts.excerpt: A 0.1-second speed-up lifted retail conversions 8.4% in a Deloitte study. What slow pages cost in sales, ad spend, leads and search, and where to start.
blogPosts.content:
Teams spend weeks polishing a hero animation and arguing over the exact shade of a gradient. Then they ship it on a page that takes four seconds to become usable on a mid-range phone, and wonder why conversions drift down every quarter.

Speed is not a developer chore. It is a line on the balance sheet. Every extra fraction of a second shows up somewhere: in checkout completions, in cost per acquisition, in whether a paid visitor ever sees your form. This post collects the numbers that are actually backed by research, so you can treat performance as a revenue metric rather than a nice-to-have.

## The short version

- A **0.1-second** improvement in mobile site speed lifted retail conversions by **8.4%** and travel conversions by **10.1%** (Deloitte for Google, 37 brands).
- When a mobile page takes **3 seconds** to load instead of 1, the probability of a bounce rises by **32%**. At **5 seconds** it rises by **90%** (Google).
- B2B sites that load in **1 second** convert about **3x** better than sites that load in 5 seconds (Portent, 2022).
- Core Web Vitals are part of how Google judges page experience, and on Google Play, apps above the crash and freeze thresholds become harder to find.

## A tenth of a second, measured

The most useful study here is “Milliseconds Make Millions”, run by Deloitte and 55 for Google. Over four weeks they tracked 37 retail, travel, luxury and lead-generation brands in Europe and the US, and measured what happened when mobile load times improved by just 0.1 seconds.

- **Retail conversions rose 8.4%.**
- **Retail average order value rose 9.2%.** People did not only buy more often, they spent more.
- **Travel conversions rose 10.1%**, the most speed-sensitive category in the study.

A tenth of a second is shorter than a blink. Amazon's often-quoted rule of thumb from its early experiments points the same way: roughly 1% of sales lost for every extra 100 milliseconds.

To make that concrete, take a store doing $500,000 a month online. If a faster mobile site delivered just a quarter of the uplift Deloitte measured, about 2% more conversions, that is roughly **$10,000 a month, or $120,000 a year**, before you touch pricing, ad spend or product mix. Your number will be different. The direction will not.

The uncomfortable takeaway for design-led teams: a fast page with a simpler design will usually out-convert a slow page with a prettier one.

## Paying for clicks that never land

Google's mobile benchmark data shows how quickly patience runs out:

- As load time goes from 1 to 3 seconds, the probability of a bounce increases **32%**.
- From 1 to 5 seconds, it increases **90%**.

Now follow the money. You pay for a click on a competitive keyword. The visitor lands, but the headline has not painted, the form has not rendered and your analytics tag has not fired. They leave. The ad platform reports a click; your analytics reports nothing, because the visitor was gone before the tag loaded. The spend looks wasted on bad traffic, when really your own site could not receive it.

Spending more on ads does not fix a leaky page. Stopping the leak does. A landing page that renders its key content in under two seconds turns the same budget into measurable sessions and conversions, and your cost per acquisition drops without touching the campaign.

## B2B: slow pages lose leads

In B2B the deals are larger and the sales cycles longer, so every lost lead hurts more. Portent's 2022 study of more than 100 million page views found that a B2B site loading in **1 second** converts about **3x** better than one loading in 5 seconds, and about **5x** better than one loading in 10 seconds.

There is a credibility effect too. A CTO evaluating your platform is quietly evaluating your engineering. A six-second load time tells them, before they read a single feature page, that performance is not a priority for your team. That is not the first impression you want when you are asking someone to trust you with their data or an annual contract.

## Search visibility and Core Web Vitals

Google measures real-user experience with Core Web Vitals, judged at the 75th percentile of visits:

- **Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)**: when the main content appears. Good is **2.5 seconds or less**. Heavy hero images, render-blocking CSS and slow servers push it up.
- **Interaction to Next Paint (INP)**: how quickly the page responds to taps and clicks. Good is **200 milliseconds or less**. INP replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 and is much stricter about long JavaScript tasks.
- **Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)**: how much the layout jumps while loading. Good is **0.1 or less**.

To be precise about rankings: Google says relevance comes first, and a great page experience will not rescue weak content. But page experience is one of the things its ranking systems reward, and when several pages answer a query equally well, the fast and stable one has the edge. Server-rendered pages also hand crawlers ready HTML, which helps large or JavaScript-heavy sites get indexed faster.

## The same math applies to mobile apps

Apps pay the same tax in different places: cold-start time, frozen screens, crashes and store ratings. Google Play makes it explicit. If more than **1.09%** of daily active users hit a noticeable crash, or more than **0.47%** hit an "App Not Responding" freeze, your app crosses Play's bad-behavior threshold and is likely to be less discoverable. Cross it on specific phone models and Play may also show users a warning on your store listing.

A slow app rarely gets a second launch. Measure start-up time and crash-free sessions as seriously as you measure page speed.

## Where the time actually goes

The instinct when a site is slow is to buy a bigger server. That is rarely the right first move. Most performance problems are architectural, and a bigger server will not fix a 3 MB JavaScript bundle. These fixes move the needle first:

- **Ship less JavaScript.** Every library is downloaded, parsed and executed on someone's phone. Swap the carousel library for CSS scroll-snap, the date-picker package for a native input, the animation framework for the four transitions you actually use.
- **Render on the server.** With frameworks like Next.js the browser receives a real page instead of an empty shell and a script tag. Content appears sooner, crawlers get HTML, and only the interactive parts hydrate.
- **Audit third-party scripts.** Tag managers, chat widgets, heatmaps and A/B testing tools often cost more than your own code. Keep the ones that earn their weight and load the rest after the page is usable.
- **Fix images and fonts.** Serve AVIF or WebP, set explicit dimensions to prevent layout shift, lazy-load below the fold, and subset and preload fonts.
- **Look at the backend.** A slow first byte usually means unindexed queries, N+1 database calls or missing caching. No amount of frontend tuning hides a 1.5-second API response.

None of this needs a bigger server. It needs discipline at the architecture level, where decisions are made once and pay off on every page view and every app launch.

## Measure it in 15 minutes

- **PageSpeed Insights**: real-user Core Web Vitals for your URL (from the Chrome UX Report) plus a Lighthouse lab test.
- **Search Console, Core Web Vitals report**: which groups of pages fail, on mobile and on desktop.
- **Your browser's Network tab**: sort by size and see what you actually ship.
- **For apps**: Android vitals in Google Play Console, and the Xcode Organizer for launch time, hangs and crashes on iOS.

## Sources

- [Deloitte & 55 for Google: Milliseconds Make Millions](https://web.dev/case-studies/milliseconds-make-millions)
- [Google: Mobile page speed industry benchmarks](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/marketing-strategies/app-and-mobile/mobile-page-speed-new-industry-benchmarks/)
- [Portent: Site speed and conversion rate research (2022)](https://www.portent.com/blog/analytics/research-site-speed-hurting-everyones-revenue.htm)
- [web.dev: Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)
- [Google Search Central: Understanding page experience](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/page-experience)
- [Android Developers: Android vitals](https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/vitals)

## Want a second opinion?

If the audit surfaces work you don't have the bandwidth for, that is what we do. ALAZ builds and fixes [web applications, mobile apps and the backends behind them](/services): server-first architecture, disciplined bundle budgets, fast APIs, and apps that stay under the stores' crash thresholds.

Send a URL or an app store link to [hello@alaz.pro](mailto:hello@alaz.pro), plus a Lighthouse report if you have one. We will tell you plainly what is slow, what it is likely costing you and what it takes to fix.

blogPosts.title: We're Live: A Software Studio for Web, Mobile and the Systems Behind Them
blogPosts.excerpt: ALAZ is open. Why we build web apps, mobile apps and backend systems as one team, how we work, and who we're a good fit for.
blogPosts.content:
ALAZ is open for business. We are a software studio that designs and builds web applications, iOS and Android apps, and the backend systems that keep them running, as one team, from the first sketch to production. This first post explains why we exist, how we work and who we are a good fit for.

## Why we started ALAZ

We have spent years untangling software that should have been simple. Bloated web bundles. Apps that freeze on a mid-range phone. Integrations that fail silently at 3 a.m. Dashboards that take six seconds to become usable and still ship to production.

Most of that pain is not a technology problem. It is a discipline problem, and very often a handover problem. The web agency, the mobile freelancer and the backend vendor each optimize their own piece, and the bugs live in the seams between them. Decisions get made once under deadline pressure, then frozen, and every new feature pays the tax.

ALAZ exists to stop paying that tax by putting the whole product, web, mobile and backend, in the hands of one accountable engineering team.

## What we build

- **Web applications.** SaaS platforms, customer portals, admin panels, internal tools and fast marketing sites. Server-first, typed end to end, and built to pass Core Web Vitals on real devices, not just in a demo.
- **Mobile applications.** iOS and Android apps from a single cross-platform codebase (Flutter or React Native), with native Swift or Kotlin where the hardware demands it. Offline-first data, push notifications and App Store and Google Play releases included.
- **Systems and backend.** The APIs your apps talk to, integrations with payment, CRM and ERP systems, background jobs, cloud infrastructure, CI/CD and monitoring.
- **Rescue and performance work.** Slow pages, crashing apps and legacy code nobody wants to touch, stabilized and modernized step by step instead of rewritten in one risky leap.

The [services page](/services) lists the deliverables and the stack behind each one.

## How we engineer

We build against a short list of convictions.

- **Speed is a feature.** Performance budgets are agreed in the first sprint, not bolted on before launch: LCP and INP targets for web, start-up time and crash-free sessions for mobile, response times for APIs.
- **Types everywhere.** TypeScript on the web and the server; Dart, Swift or Kotlin on mobile. Types catch the bugs that reviews miss and let us refactor without flinching.
- **Boring technology, on purpose.** Mature tools and predictable patterns mean we can reason about the system at 2 a.m. when something breaks.
- **Small, replaceable pieces.** Requirements always change. Modular systems absorb the change; monoliths make you pay for it.
- **You own everything.** Code, cloud accounts, app store listings and documentation belong to you from day one. No lock-in.

None of this is exotic. The bar is low because most teams optimize for the demo. We optimize for month eighteen.

## What working with us looks like

- **Discovery call (30 to 45 minutes).** What you are building, who it is for, and what it costs the business if it fails.
- **Written scope and estimate.** A short, plain document: what we will build, what we will deliberately leave out, the phases, the timeline and the price. Not a 40-page proposal.
- **Build in short increments.** Working software every week or two: a staging link for web, a TestFlight or internal testing build for mobile. You see progress, not slide decks.
- **Launch and handover.** A zero-downtime release, monitoring, documentation and a walkthrough for your team, with the option to keep us on for maintenance.

## Who we are a good fit for

- Founders turning a prototype or an idea into a real web or mobile product.
- Companies replacing spreadsheets and brittle legacy tools with software built around their workflow.
- Teams whose site is slow, whose app crashes, or whose integrations keep breaking.
- Businesses that want a long-term technical partner, not a vendor that disappears after launch.

## Say hello

Tell us what you are building and what is in the way. Write to [hello@alaz.pro](mailto:hello@alaz.pro) or use the [project form](/start-project). Every message is read by an engineer, and we reply within one business day.

We are live. Tell us what you are building.

faqs.q: How is ALAZ different from a digital agency?
faqs.a: ALAZ is run by engineers. The people who scope your project are the people who write the web and mobile code and design the backend, so nothing gets lost between a sales team and a delivery team. We also ship our own products, Vocabulary and Market Hours, so we know what it takes to keep software running after launch.

faqs.q: Do you build apps for both iOS and Android?
faqs.a: Yes. Most projects use one cross-platform codebase (Flutter or React Native) that ships to both the App Store and Google Play. Where a feature needs deep device access, we add native Swift or Kotlin modules. We also handle store accounts, submission and review.

faqs.q: How long does a project take?
faqs.a: A focused MVP or internal tool, web or mobile, usually takes 4 to 8 weeks from kick-off to production, plus store review time for mobile apps. Platforms with several apps and integrations take 2 to 4 months. After discovery you get a concrete timeline with phased deliverables.

faqs.q: How much does a web or mobile app cost?
faqs.a: It depends on scope, integrations and the number of user roles, which is why we scope before we quote. As a guide, the budget ranges on our project form start under $25k for a focused tool or MVP and go above $100k for a multi-app platform. You get a written price with phases, not an hourly meter.

Proven, stable tools over hype cycles. Web: TypeScript, Next.js, React and Node.js. Mobile: Flutter or React Native, with Swift and Kotlin where needed. Data and infrastructure: PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker and AWS or GCP. If your team already has a stack, we can work in it.

faqs.q: Do we own the source code after delivery?
faqs.a: Yes, completely. Every line of code, infrastructure configuration, app store listing and document belongs to you from day one. There is no proprietary platform and no lock-in.

faqs.q: Can you take over or rescue an existing product?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly audit slow, unstable or poorly structured web apps, mobile apps and backends. We profile them, fix the critical bottlenecks and restore stability without forcing an expensive, risky ground-up rewrite.

faqs.q: Do you support the product after launch?
faqs.a: Yes. We can stay on for maintenance (monitoring, security and dependency updates, OS upgrades for mobile, and new features), or hand everything over to your team with documentation and a walkthrough.

faqs.q: Do you work with clients outside Türkiye?
faqs.a: Yes. We work in English and Turkish from İzmir and New York, which covers European and US working hours, and most of our communication happens asynchronously in writing with a weekly call.

heading: THE WORKING
FLAME
about.introText: ALAZ is a small software studio in İzmir and New York. We design and build web applications, iOS and Android apps, and the APIs and infrastructure behind them, and we ship our own products so we know what it takes to keep software running after launch.
about.originDefinition: The bright, working part of a flame: not the first spark and not the ember, but the heat that actually shapes metal.
originParagraphs: Alaz is an old Turkish word for the working part of a fire, the moment it stops just burning and gets hot enough to shape something. That is the part of the work we care about.

Generating activity is easy: more code, more features, more meetings. Getting a system to hold up under real users and real traffic is the hard part, and that is the bar every project has to clear before we call it finished.
about.processEyebrowRight: THE SAME FOUR STEPS, EVERY PROJECT

processSteps.title: DISCOVERY
processSteps.body: A 30 to 45 minute call: who is going to use this, what it costs the business if it fails, and what to leave out on purpose. That homework happens before anyone opens an editor.

processSteps.title: SCOPE
processSteps.body: A system exists on a whiteboard before it exists in a repo. You get a short written scope with phases, a timeline and a price, and we only start when it is agreed.

processSteps.title: BUILD
processSteps.body: Working software every week or two: a staging link for web, a TestFlight or internal testing build for mobile. Each piece is tested and trusted on its own before the next one lands.

processSteps.title: LAUNCH
processSteps.body: Shipping is the halfway point. A zero-downtime release, monitoring, documentation your team can actually use, and a walkthrough, with the option to keep us on for maintenance.

about.productsText: Client work is most of what we do, but we also build and run our own products. They keep us honest about launch day, store reviews, support and month eighteen.

meta.title: Legal
meta.description: Terms for using alaz.pro: who runs the site, what you may do with it, intellectual property, liability and governing law.

sections.heading: Who we are
sections.body: alaz.pro is run by ALAZ, a small software engineering studio with offices in the United States and Türkiye. You can find the addresses and contact details in the footer and on the About page.

sections.heading: Using this website
sections.body: You're welcome to browse the site and send us a project inquiry. Please don't scrape it at scale, probe it for weaknesses without asking us first, or use it for anything unlawful. We may change or take down parts of the site at any time without notice.

sections.heading: No agreement by inquiry
sections.body: Sending an inquiry doesn't create a contract, and we don't promise to take every project on. Scope, price, timeline and deliverables are only binding once both sides sign a separate written agreement.

sections.heading: Information on the site
sections.body: We try to keep things accurate, but the content is general information and is provided as is, without warranties of any kind. Case studies and blog posts reflect our experience and opinions at the time of writing; they aren't advice for your specific situation.

sections.heading: Intellectual property
sections.body: The text, design, code and media on this site belong to ALAZ or are used with permission, unless noted otherwise. Names and logos of clients or tools we mention belong to their owners. Please ask before reusing our material.

sections.heading: Links to other sites
sections.body: We may link to third-party sites. We don't control them and aren't responsible for what they say or how they handle your data.

sections.heading: Liability
sections.body: To the extent the law allows, ALAZ isn't liable for losses that result from using this website or relying on its content. Nothing here limits liability that can't legally be limited.

sections.heading: Governing law
sections.body: These terms are governed by the laws of the Republic of Türkiye. Courts in İzmir have jurisdiction, unless mandatory consumer rules in your country say otherwise.

sections.heading: Changes and questions
sections.body: We may update this page from time to time; the date at the top shows the latest version. Questions? Write to hello@alaz.pro.

meta.title: Privacy
meta.description: How ALAZ handles the information you send through the project form: what we collect, why, who sees it, how long we keep it and your rights.

sections.heading: What we collect
sections.body: Only what you give us through the project inquiry form: your name, email address, company, and the details of your project. Our servers also keep basic technical logs (IP address, browser, requested page) for security and troubleshooting.

sections.heading: Why we use it
sections.body: To read your inquiry, reply to you, and talk through a possible project. We don't use it for advertising, and we don't sell it or rent it out.

sections.heading: Who sees it
sections.body: The people at ALAZ who handle inquiries, plus the hosting and email providers that run our systems on our behalf. They may only process your data for that purpose. We'll disclose information if a court or authority legally requires it.

sections.heading: Cookies and tracking
sections.body: The site doesn't use advertising or analytics cookies. If that changes, we'll update this page and ask for consent where the law requires it.

sections.heading: How long we keep it
sections.body: Inquiries are kept while we're talking to you and for a reasonable period afterwards, then deleted. If we end up working together, project records are kept as long as the contract and the law require.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: Depending on where you live (for example under the GDPR, the UK GDPR, Turkey's KVKK, or US state privacy laws), you can ask to see, correct, export or delete your data, or object to how we use it. Email hello@alaz.pro and we'll answer within 30 days. You can also complain to your local data protection authority.

sections.heading: Security
sections.body: We use encrypted connections and restrict access to the data. No system is perfectly secure, so we can't guarantee absolute protection, but we take reasonable steps to keep your information safe.

sections.heading: Children
sections.body: The site is meant for businesses and adults. We don't knowingly collect data from anyone under 16.

sections.heading: Changes
sections.body: If we change how we handle your data, we'll update this page and the date above.
